note: The history rail on the home page. Each pin is coloured by the same engine as the stages: parts are [colorantId, concentration] pairs through Beer–Lambert at the given thickness, or a dichroic band at an angle. A pin with no colour is one the engine cannot model yet. stage is the id of the home-page section that explains it.

pins.title: Cobalt blue in Egypt
pins.text: Glass of Egypt's 18th Dynasty is already coloured with cobalt, the same ion as in a modern blue rod. Cobalt was used as a blue on pottery of the same period too.
sources: Internet Archaeology 52: cobalt-blue glass of the 18th Dynasty

pins.title: The Lycurgus cup
pins.text: A Roman cage cup that looks jade green in reflected light and glows red when lit from inside. About 330 ppm of silver and 40 ppm of gold sit in it as particles about 70 nm across. The pin shows the transmitted colour; the green is scattered light, which this engine does not model.

pins.title: Forest glass
pins.text: North of the Alps, glass was melted in woodland furnaces with potash from wood ash. Iron in the sand and the furnace atmosphere left it green, from pale to deep.

pins.title: Venetian cristallo
pins.text: Angelo Barovier of Murano is credited with a nearly colourless glass. Small additions of manganese oxide cancel the iron's tint: manganese absorbs in the green, iron at the ends, and together they take a little of everything, which reads as clear.

pins.title: Gold ruby
pins.text: In 1676 the Hamburg physician Andreas Cassius reported the red that gold chloride gives. By about 1679 Johann Kunckel was making ruby glass in Potsdam and keeping the recipe secret. It comes out of the melt grey and turns red only on reheating.

pins.title: Uranium glass
pins.text: In Bohemia, Franz Xaver Riedel named his uranium yellow and yellow-green glasses annagelb and annagrün after his daughter. In the US, production stopped in 1942 when uranium went to the Manhattan Project. Under ultraviolet light it glows green: it gives light out instead of taking it away, so this absorption-only engine cannot colour its pin.

pins.title: Didymium split in two
pins.text: Carl Auer von Welsbach separated didymium, named in 1841 as one element, into neodymium and praseodymium. Didymium glasses need both to block the sodium flare.

pins.title: Selenium red
pins.text: Franz Welz patented selenium, with cadmium, as a red for glass. It was cheaper than gold ruby and went into railway signal lenses by the early 1900s. The source here is a collectors' history, so treat the year as approximate.

pins.title: Crookes's eye-preserving glass
pins.text: On 10 November 1913 the Royal Society's Glassworkers' Cataract Committee adopted William Crookes's report on "eye-preserving glass for spectacles". His glasses used iron to absorb a furnace's infrared.
sources: Royal Society archive: committee minutes, 10 Nov 1913

pins.title: The interference filter
pins.text: Walter Geffcken at Schott in Jena filed a patent for a light filter made of stacked thin films. Dichroic art glass is often credited to NASA, but the multilayer filter behind it is older.
